idiom_name: standalone functions typed against a structural capability interface
implementation_notes: The TypeScript servant is a plain function whose parameter type is a narrow interface, export function moveTo(shape: Movable, to: Position), so the capability contract is checked at compile time and erased at runtime - the closest thing to the classic structure with no ceremony, because structural typing means no class has to declare conformance explicitly. When the behaviour must appear as a member, the language offers mixin class expressions (a factory returning a subclass over a base class) rather than prototype patching; module augmentation and interface merging can add types but not implementations, and decorators attach only to declarations you control. The classic servant class is rarely warranted and never for stateless behaviour; keep an object only when the servant holds configuration, caches results, or must be swapped in tests.
pitfalls: Interfaces are erased: a servant typed against Movable still fails at runtime for an object that only claims conformance (any, assertion), and the failure surfaces inside the servant - validate untrusted input at the boundary with a type guard.

Installing methods with Object.assign(Shape.prototype, ...) is the JavaScript trap in TypeScript clothing: the compiler never sees the added member, name clashes silently overwrite, and declaration merging cannot add the implementation.

A structural capability interface accepts objects that merely have a compatible shape: an unrelated object with a position field becomes 'servable', so document the semantic requirement, not just the shape.
sources: TypeScript documentation, Mixins - the class-expression pattern for adding behaviour to classes at the type level and at runtime; https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/mixins

TypeScript documentation, Classes - implements clauses check that a class satisfies an interface, and the caution that the clause changes nothing about the class's type; https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/2/classes.html
